questions.q: What is the necessary condition for adding two matrices \(A\) and \(B\)? State the condition precisely.
questions.a: The matrices must have the same order (same number of rows and same number of columns). If \(A\) is \(m \times n\) and \(B\) is \(p \times q\), then \(m = p\) and \(n = q\). A wrong answer (e.g., "same number of elements" or "both square") reveals the student confuses total element count with order matching, or thinks only square matrices can be added.

questions.q: Explain why the sum of a \(2 \times 3\) matrix and a \(3 \times 2\) matrix is not defined, even though both have 6 elements.
questions.a: Matrix addition requires corresponding positions to represent the same quantity. In a \(2 \times 3\) matrix, the element at \((1,2)\) might be "boys' shoes in category 2", while in a \(3 \times 2\) matrix the element at \((1,2)\) could be "girls' shoes in category 1". The positions do not align, so adding them would mix unrelated data. A student who says "they have the same number of elements so it should work" misunderstands that order encodes meaning, not just size.

questions.q: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 4 \\ 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\). Compute \(A + B\) and \(A - B\). Show all steps.
questions.a:
\(A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 2+(-3) & -1+4 \\ 0+5 & 3+(-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).  
\(A - B = \begin{bmatrix} 2-(-3) & -1-4 \\ 0-5 & 3-(-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -5 \\ -5 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).  
A wrong answer often comes from sign errors (e.g., \(2-(-3) = -1\)) or subtracting in the wrong order (\(B - A\) instead of \(A - B\)). This reveals carelessness with integer signs or confusion about non-commutativity of subtraction.

questions.q: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 10 \\ 11 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\), verify the associative property \((A+B)+C = A+(B+C)\) by computing both sides. What does this tell you about writing \(A+B+C\) without parentheses?
questions.a:
\((A+B)+C = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 8 \\ 10 & 12 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 10 \\ 11 & 12 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 18 \\ 21 & 24 \end{bmatrix}\).  
\(A+(B+C) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 16 \\ 18 & 20 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 18 \\ 21 & 24 \end{bmatrix}\).  
Both sides are equal, so matrix addition is associative. Therefore \(A+B+C\) can be written without parentheses. A student who gets different results likely made an arithmetic error or added rows to columns incorrectly. This tests whether they can systematically apply element-wise addition across three matrices.

questions.q: A student solves \(X + \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) by writing \(X = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 1 \\ 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\). Is this correct? If not, identify the error and give the correct \(X\).
questions.a: The student incorrectly added the matrix instead of subtracting it. The correct step is \(X = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). The error shows the student treats matrix equations exactly like scalar equations but forgets that moving a term to the other side requires adding its additive inverse (i.e., subtracting). This is a classic sign error when transposing matrix terms.

questions.q: Create a real-world problem (with an Indian context, e.g., a school canteen, a farm, or a small business) that requires adding two matrices of order \(2 \times 3\). Write the problem statement, define the matrices, and show the addition.
questions.a: A good answer will: (1) describe two entities (e.g., two school canteens) with the same categories (rows) and items (columns), (2) give numerical data for each, (3) represent them as \(2 \times 3\) matrices, (4) add them element-wise, and (5) interpret the result (e.g., total weekly sales). A poor answer might use different categories for the two matrices, mismatch orders, or fail to explain what rows/columns represent. This reveals whether the student understands that addition combines *comparable* data.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine two shoe factories, Factory A and Factory B, each producing boys' and girls' shoes in three price ______.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Matrix addition?
questions.a: Students frequently attempt to add matrices of different orders, arguing that "both have 6 elements".

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can also model real-world situations (e.g., combined sales, change in production) using matrix addition/subtraction.
